claim: Mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) are capable of generating most cell types that constitute the entire organism
source: Mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs), capable of generating most cell types that constitute the entire organism, have made important contributions to our understanding of mammalian biology (Smith, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith, 2001

claim: Neural induction requires active FGF signaling
source: Neural induction, the first step in neural differentiation of mESCs, requires active FGF signaling (Ying et al., 2003) and inhibition of the BMP/TGF-beta pathway (Chambers et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ying et al., 2003

claim: Neural induction requires inhibition of the BMP/TGF-beta pathway
source: Neural induction, the first step in neural differentiation of mESCs, requires active FGF signaling (Ying et al., 2003) and inhibition of the BMP/TGF-beta pathway (Chambers et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chambers et al., 2009

claim: Regional identity and lineage-guided differentiation are regulated by the presence or absence of various morphogens or transcription factors
source: Subsequent regional identity and lineage-guided differentiation are further regulated by the presence or absence of various morphogens or transcription factors (Lee et al., 2000; Wichterle et al., 2002; Andersson et al., 2006; Martinat et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Lee et al., 2000; Wichterle et al., 2002; Andersson et al., 2006; Martinat et al., 2006

claim: A relatively low and consistent number of TH+ neurons were detected in the mESC monolayer culture system
source: Finally, our adaptation of the mESC monolayer culture and differentiation method (Ying and Smith, 2003) showed that a relatively low and consistent number of TH+ neurons were detected in the culture system (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1 and citation to Ying and Smith, 2003

claim: E14 mESC cultures express neural progenitor markers (Sox2, Lmx1A, and Nestin) after 7-day stage one culture
source: E14 mESC cultures express neural progenitor makers (Sox2, Lmx1A, and Nestin) after 7-day stage one culture.
evidence: Supported by Figure 1B showing immunostaining results

claim: 46C mESC cultures are GFP positive after 7-day stage one culture
source: 46C mESC cultures, in which GFP is driven by the sox1 promoter, are GFP positive after 7-day stage one culture.
evidence: Supported by Figure 1B showing GFP expression

claim: All coefficient of variation (C.V.) values but one were smaller than 20%
source: To assess assay performance, the coefficient of variation (C.V.) of DMSO control was calculated for each of the twenty-six 96-well plates screened, and all C.V.s but one were smaller than 20%, suggesting an acceptable variation during this cell-based screen (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1D showing C.V. data

claim: Out of 2080 chemicals screened, 26 led to a fold change of TH+ cells larger than mean + 3 S.D. (1.16%)
source: Out of 2080 chemicals screened, 26 led to a fold change of TH+ cells larger than mean + 3 S.D. (1.16%) (Figure 1E for an example), and 20 out of the 26 were neither cytotoxic nor auto-fluorescent (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by screening data and Figure 1E-F

claim: 20 out of the 26 primary hits were neither cytotoxic nor auto-fluorescent
source: Out of 2080 chemicals screened, 26 led to a fold change of TH+ cells larger than mean + 3 S.D. (1.16%) (Figure 1E for an example), and 20 out of the 26 were neither cytotoxic nor auto-fluorescent (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by screening data and Figure 1F

claim: The overall hit rate was 0.09%
source: After two rounds of validation, two compounds were selected as hits, yielding an overall hit rate of 0.09%.
evidence: Calculated from screening results: 2 hits out of 2080 compounds

claim: Dihydrodeoxygedunin (DOG) is a natural product with known neurotrophic activity via activating the TrkB receptor and its downstream signaling cascades
source: One identified molecule is Dihydrodeoxygedunin (DOG), which is a natural product with known neurotrophic activity via activating the TrkB receptor and its downstream signaling cascades (Jang et al., 2010a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jang et al., 2010a

claim: Both DOG and 7,8-dihydroxyflavone (DHF) increased TH+ cells in mESC cultures, albeit modestly
source: Both DOG and 7,8-dihydroxyflavone (DHF, another selective TrkB agonist [Jang et al., 2010b]) increased TH+ cells in mESC cultures, albeit modestly (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by Figure 2 showing experimental results

claim: Treatment with selamectin increased the percentage of total neurons, compared to the DMSO-treated control
source: Treatment with selamectin increased the percentage of total neurons, compared to the DMSO-treated control (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Supported by Figure 3A-B showing NeuN immunostaining results

claim: Selamectin significantly increased the production of 5-HT neurons
source: Further analysis showed that selamectin also significantly increased the production of 5-HT neurons (Figure 3C), GABAergic neurons (Figure 3D), and Islet+ motor neurons (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by Figure 3C showing 5-HT immunostaining results

claim: Selamectin significantly increased the production of GABAergic neurons
source: Further analysis showed that selamectin also significantly increased the production of 5-HT neurons (Figure 3C), GABAergic neurons (Figure 3D), and Islet+ motor neurons (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by Figure 3D showing GABA immunostaining results

claim: Selamectin significantly increased the production of Islet+ motor neurons
source: Further analysis showed that selamectin also significantly increased the production of 5-HT neurons (Figure 3C), GABAergic neurons (Figure 3D), and Islet+ motor neurons (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by Figure 3E showing Islet immunostaining results

claim: The increase of 5-HT neurons was remarkably high (∼sevenfold)
source: The increase of 5-HT neurons was remarkably high (∼sevenfold), suggesting that selamectin might have a preferential activity for inducing 5-HT neurons.
evidence: Supported by quantification of 5-HT neurons in Figure 3C

claim: Selamectin might have a preferential activity for inducing 5-HT neurons
source: The increase of 5-HT neurons was remarkably high (∼sevenfold), suggesting that selamectin might have a preferential activity for inducing 5-HT neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the sevenfold increase in 5-HT neurons

claim: The percentage of Oligo2+ cells increased after treatment with selamectin compared with the DMSO-treated control
source: After treatment with selamectin, the percentage of Oligo2+ cells also increased compared with the DMSO-treated control (Figure 3F), suggesting that the increase of neuronal production is not at the expense of glial production.
evidence: Supported by Figure 3F showing Olig2 immunostaining results

claim: The increase of neuronal production is not at the expense of glial production
source: After treatment with selamectin, the percentage of Oligo2+ cells also increased compared with the DMSO-treated control (Figure 3F), suggesting that the increase of neuronal production is not at the expense of glial production.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both neurons and oligodendrocytes increased

claim: Selamectin functions in a dose-dependent manner with an EC50 = 293 nM
source: The result showed that selamectin functions in a dose-dependent manner with an effector concentration for half-maximum response EC50 = 293 nM (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by dose-response curve in Figure 4A

claim: Selamectin is toxic above 500 nM
source: When the concentration of selamectin was higher than 500 nM, it became toxic to cells.
evidence: Observed from dose-response experiments

claim: Treatment during Stage one (from Day 4 to Day 7) suppressed cell proliferation
source: Treatment during Stage one (from Day 4 to Day 7, mainly composed of undifferentiated ESCs) suppressed cell proliferation, resulting in insufficient number of cells on Day 7 for further evaluation.
evidence: Observed from time course experiments

claim: Treatment during Stage two (from Day 7 to Day 10) led to a significant increase of neurons evaluated on Day 13
source: Treatment during Stage two (from Day 7 to Day 10, mainly composed of neural progenitors) led to a significant increase of neurons evaluated on Day 13 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by Figure 4B showing time course results

claim: Shortening the treatment regimen to one day (from Day 7 to Day 8) showed no significant effect of selamectin
source: Shortening the treatment regimen to one day (i.e., from Day 7 to Day 8) or treatment during Stage three (from Day 10 to Day 13, mainly composed of differentiating neurons) showed no significant effect of selamectin (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by Figure 4B showing time course results

claim: Treatment during Stage three (from Day 10 to Day 13) showed no significant effect of selamectin
source: Shortening the treatment regimen to one day (i.e., from Day 7 to Day 8) or treatment during Stage three (from Day 10 to Day 13, mainly composed of differentiating neurons) showed no significant effect of selamectin (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by Figure 4B showing time course results

claim: Selamectin's proneurogenic activity is likely due to its action on mESC-derived neural progenitors
source: These results suggest that selamectin's proneurogenic activity is likely due to its action on mESC-derived neural progenitors.
evidence: Inferred from time course experiments showing effect only during neural progenitor stage

claim: Selamectin belongs to a chemical family of macrocyclic lactones used to treat nematode infections
source: Selamectin belongs to a chemical family of macrocyclic lactones used to treat nematode infections that cause onchocerciasis (also known as the river blindness) in humans (Goa et al., 1991) and as topical or oral parasiticide and antihelminthic on dogs and cats (Bishop et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goa et al., 1991 and Bishop et al., 2000

claim: Macrocyclic lactones disable parasites by displacing glutamate in their muscle synapses through acting on the glutamate-gated chloride (GluCl) channels
source: This class of drugs disables parasites by displacing glutamate in their muscle synapses through acting on the glutamate-gated chloride (GluCl) channels (Bloomquist, 2003), which have no orthologues in vertebrates.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bloomquist, 2003

claim: Glutamate-gated chloride (GluCl) channels have no orthologues in vertebrates
source: This class of drugs disables parasites by displacing glutamate in their muscle synapses through acting on the glutamate-gated chloride (GluCl) channels (Bloomquist, 2003), which have no orthologues in vertebrates.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bloomquist, 2003

claim: Avermectin has less potent proneurogenic activity than selamectin
source: A better-studied example of this family is avermectin (for the structures of selamectin and avermectin, Figure 5A), which, when tested for its activity in promoting neuronal differentiation, showed a less potent effect than selamectin with a marginal significance achieved at 0.25 μM (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by Figure 5B showing comparative dose-response data

claim: Vertebrate glycine channels are thought to be orthologous to the invertebrate GluCl channels
source: Based on gene structure and phylogenetic analyses, vertebrate glycine channels are thought to be orthologous to the invertebrate GluCl channels (Vassilatis et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vassilatis et al., 1997

claim: Ivermectin can act as an agonist of the glycine receptor
source: It has been reported that ivermectin (an avermectin derivative) can act as an agonist of the glycine receptor (Shan et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shan et al., 2001

claim: Non-synaptically released taurine can activate the endogenous glycine receptor during neocortical development
source: Moreover, non-synaptically released taurine can activate the endogenous glycine receptor during neocortical development (Flint et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Flint et al., 1998

claim: Taurine at a wide range of concentrations showed no effect in increasing TH% among total cells
source: We treated cells from Day 7 to Day 11 with a wide range of taurine concentrations, none of which, however, showed any effect in increasing TH% among total cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by Figure 5C showing taurine dose-response data

claim: Selamectin does not act through glycine receptors to promote neuronal differentiation from mESCs
source: This result suggests that selamectin does not act through glycine receptors to promote neuronal differentiation from mESCs.
evidence: Inferred from lack of effect of taurine, a glycine receptor agonist

claim: Avermectin can bind to the GABAA receptor in rat brain membranes or cultured cerebellar neuronal assays
source: Next we turned to another potential candidate, the GABAA receptor, since some reports in the literature suggest that avermectin can bind to the GABAA receptor in rat brain membranes or cultured cerebellar neuronal assays (Pong et al., 1982; Huang and Casida, 1997), and avermectin exhibits an anticonvulsant action in a mouse seizure model (Dawson et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pong et al., 1982 and Huang and Casida, 1997

claim: Avermectin exhibits an anticonvulsant action in a mouse seizure model
source: Next we turned to another potential candidate, the GABAA receptor, since some reports in the literature suggest that avermectin can bind to the GABAA receptor in rat brain membranes or cultured cerebellar neuronal assays (Pong et al., 1982; Huang and Casida, 1997), and avermectin exhibits an anticonvulsant action in a mouse seizure model (Dawson et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dawson et al., 2000

claim: All concentrations of Muscimol (from 1 μM to 100 μM) had proneurogenic activity like selamectin
source: We first tested the effect of the GABAA receptor agonist Muscimol at a wide range of concentrations (from 1 μM to 100 μM). Remarkably, all of them had proneurogenic activity like selamectin (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by Figure 5D showing Muscimol dose-response data

claim: Chlordiazepoxide (CDZ) at 10 μM had significant proneurogenic activity
source: When cells were treated alone with 10 μM Chlordiazepoxide or 0.3 μM Selamectin, significant proneurogenic activity was observed as compared to the DMSO control (p<0.05, t-test, Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by Figure 5E showing CDZ effect

claim: No significant additive effect was observed when cells were treated with both Selamectin (0.3 μM) and CDZ (10 μM)
source: When cells were treated with both Selamectin (0.3 μM) and CDZ (10 μM), no significant additive effect was observed (p=0.480, t-test, Figure 5F), suggesting a lack of synergistic or cooperative action between these two compounds.
evidence: Supported by Figure 5E showing combined treatment data

claim: There is a lack of synergistic or cooperative action between selamectin and chlordiazepoxide
source: When cells were treated with both Selamectin (0.3 μM) and CDZ (10 μM), no significant additive effect was observed (p=0.480, t-test, Figure 5F), suggesting a lack of synergistic or cooperative action between these two compounds.
evidence: Inferred from lack of additive effect

claim: Treatment with bicuculline, picrotoxin, or pentylenetetrazol alone had no effect on baseline differentiation of TH+ neurons
source: When cells were treated alone with these chemicals, no effect on baseline differentiation of TH+ neurons was observed, suggesting that at this stage of the mESC culture, GABA might not be released in sufficient quantities to affect neuronal differentiation (Figure 5F, white columns, all control were normalized to fold change = 1, displayed as the red dotted line).
evidence: Supported by Figure 5F showing antagonist effects

claim: At the neural progenitor stage of mESC culture, GABA might not be released in sufficient quantities to affect neuronal differentiation
source: When cells were treated alone with these chemicals, no effect on baseline differentiation of TH+ neurons was observed, suggesting that at this stage of the mESC culture, GABA might not be released in sufficient quantities to affect neuronal differentiation (Figure 5F, white columns, all control were normalized to fold change = 1, displayed as the red dotted line).
evidence: Inferred from lack of effect of GABAA receptor antagonists alone

claim: The effect of selamectin was blocked when cells were treated with selamectin together with picrotoxin, pentylenetetrazol, or bicuculline
source: When cells were treated with selamectin together with these antagonists or blockers (500 μM PTX, 5 mM PTZ, or 100 μM Bicu), the effect of selamectin was blocked, leading to no significant difference between the treated group and control (Figure 5F, gray columns).
evidence: Supported by Figure 5F showing blocking experiments

claim: The glycine receptor inhibitor strychnine failed to block the effect of selamectin
source: In contrast, the glycine receptor inhibitor strychnine (STY, 100 μM) failed to block the effect of selamectin (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by Figure 5F showing strychnine blocking experiment

claim: Selamectin promotes multi-lineage neuronal differentiation from mESCs through the activation of GABAA receptor signaling
source: Together, these pharmacological data suggest that selamectin promotes multi-lineage neuronal differentiation from mESCs through the activation of GABAA receptor signaling.
evidence: Inferred from pharmacological blocking experiments

claim: The mammalian CNS expresses nineteen GABAA receptor subunits
source: The mammalian CNS expresses nineteen GABAA receptor subunits (α1-6, β1-3, γ1-3, δ, ε, θ, π, ρ1−3), the combinatorial co-assembly of which enables a potentially enormous molecular and functional heterogeneity of GABAA receptor subtypes (Farrant and Nusser, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Farrant and Nusser, 2005

claim: Six GABAA receptor subunit genes display high expression level in mESC-derived neural progenitors
source: Through analyzing the expression profiles of all nineteen receptor subunits in mESC cultures, six genes were identified to display high expression level in mESC-derived neural progenitors (data not shown) and were therefore chosen for esiRNA knockdown.
evidence: Based on expression profiling data

claim: EsiRNAs targeting the α1, β2, γ2, and π subunits were highly effective in reducing the transcript levels of respective genes
source: Transfection of gene-specific esiRNAs on Day 6/9 and qRT-PCR analysis on Day 8/11 (Figure 6A) showed that esiRNAs targeting the α1 (encoded by the gabara1 gene), β2 (gabarb2 gene), γ2 (gabarg2), and π (gabarp gene) subunits were highly effective in reducing the transcript levels of respective genes (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by Figure 6B showing qRT-PCR results

claim: Treatment with the esiRNA targeting gabarg2 abolished the effect of selamectin in inducing NeuN+ and TH+ neurons
source: Furthermore, treatment with the esiRNA targeting gabarg2 abolished the effect of selamectin in inducing NeuN+ and TH+ neurons (Figure 6C–H).
evidence: Supported by Figure 6C-H showing knockdown results

claim: Treatment with the esiRNAs targeting gabara1, gabarb2, and gabarp genes did not noticeably block the effect of selamectin
source: Treatment with the esiRNAs targeting gabara1, gabarb2, and gabarp genes did not noticeably block the effect of selamectin, suggesting that either the reduction of transcript levels is not sufficient to abrogate their gene activity or these subunits do not mediate the effect of selamectin.
evidence: Supported by knockdown experiments in Figure 6

claim: Selamectin acts through the γ2-containing GABAA receptor to promote neuronal differentiation
source: Together, these results provide genetic evidence that selamectin acts through the γ2-containing GABAA receptor to promote neuronal differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from esiRNA knockdown experiments

claim: GABA signaling mediated by the activation of GABAA receptors can depolarize cells in the ventricular zone of the rat embryonic cortex
source: Opposite to its inhibitory roles in adult neurons, GABA signaling mediated by the activation of GABAA receptors can depolarize cells in the ventricular zone of the rat embryonic cortex (LoTurco et al., 1995), neural progenitor/stem cells in the postnatal mouse sub-ventricular zone (Liu et al., 2005) or sub-granular zone (Tozuka et al., 2005), due to the elevated internal Cl− concentrations in progenitor cells and young neurons (Owens and Kriegstein, 2002; Spitzer, 2006; Ben-Ari et al., 2007; Ge et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to LoTurco et al., 1995

claim: GABA signaling can depolarize neural progenitor/stem cells in the postnatal mouse sub-ventricular zone
source: Opposite to its inhibitory roles in adult neurons, GABA signaling mediated by the activation of GABAA receptors can depolarize cells in the ventricular zone of the rat embryonic cortex (LoTurco et al., 1995), neural progenitor/stem cells in the postnatal mouse sub-ventricular zone (Liu et al., 2005) or sub-granular zone (Tozuka et al., 2005), due to the elevated internal Cl− concentrations in progenitor cells and young neurons (Owens and Kriegstein, 2002; Spitzer, 2006; Ben-Ari et al., 2007; Ge et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2005

claim: GABA signaling can depolarize neural progenitor/stem cells in the postnatal mouse sub-granular zone
source: Opposite to its inhibitory roles in adult neurons, GABA signaling mediated by the activation of GABAA receptors can depolarize cells in the ventricular zone of the rat embryonic cortex (LoTurco et al., 1995), neural progenitor/stem cells in the postnatal mouse sub-ventricular zone (Liu et al., 2005) or sub-granular zone (Tozuka et al., 2005), due to the elevated internal Cl− concentrations in progenitor cells and young neurons (Owens and Kriegstein, 2002; Spitzer, 2006; Ben-Ari et al., 2007; Ge et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tozuka et al., 2005

claim: GABA depolarization is due to the elevated internal Cl− concentrations in progenitor cells and young neurons
source: Opposite to its inhibitory roles in adult neurons, GABA signaling mediated by the activation of GABAA receptors can depolarize cells in the ventricular zone of the rat embryonic cortex (LoTurco et al., 1995), neural progenitor/stem cells in the postnatal mouse sub-ventricular zone (Liu et al., 2005) or sub-granular zone (Tozuka et al., 2005), due to the elevated internal Cl− concentrations in progenitor cells and young neurons (Owens and Kriegstein, 2002; Spitzer, 2006; Ben-Ari et al., 2007; Ge et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Owens and Kriegstein, 2002; Spitzer, 2006; Ben-Ari et al., 2007; Ge et al., 2007

claim: Neural rosettes are a functionally distinct type of neural stem cells suggested to represent the earliest NSC stage in vivo
source: Based on the observed temporal effect of selamectin in mESC cultures, we focused our attention on neural rosettes, a functionally distinct type of neural stem cells suggested to represent the earliest NSC stage in vivo (Elkabetz et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Elkabetz et al., 2008

claim: Neural rosettes are easily recognizable because of their characteristic bipolar morphology and radial floral-like arrangement
source: Neural rosettes are easily recognizable because of their characteristic bipolar morphology and radial floral-like arrangement.
evidence: Based on morphological observations

claim: For neural rosettes, membrane capacitance Cm = 9.4 ± 12.5 pF (mean ± S.D., n = 106)
source: For neural rosettes, we observed membrane capacitance Cm = 9.4 ± 12.5 pF (mean ± S.D., n = 106), input resistance Rm = 772.5 ± 1037.1 MΩ (mean ± S.D., n = 106), and resting membrane potential ERev = − 20.9 ± 8.3 mV (mean ± S.D., n = 71).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings

claim: For neural rosettes, input resistance Rm = 772.5 ± 1037.1 MΩ (mean ± S.D., n = 106)
source: For neural rosettes, we observed membrane capacitance Cm = 9.4 ± 12.5 pF (mean ± S.D., n = 106), input resistance Rm = 772.5 ± 1037.1 MΩ (mean ± S.D., n = 106), and resting membrane potential ERev = − 20.9 ± 8.3 mV (mean ± S.D., n = 71).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings

source: For neural rosettes, we observed membrane capacitance Cm = 9.4 ± 12.5 pF (mean ± S.D., n = 106), input resistance Rm = 772.5 ± 1037.1 MΩ (mean ± S.D., n = 106), and resting membrane potential ERev = − 20.9 ± 8.3 mV (mean ± S.D., n = 71).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings

claim: For non-rosette cells, membrane capacitance Cm = 9.5 ± 6.2 pF (mean ± S.D., n = 74)
source: For non-rosette cells, we observed membrane capacitance Cm = 9.5 ± 6.2 pF (mean ± S.D., n = 74), input resistance Rm = 1.2 ± 1.2 GΩ (mean ± S.D., n = 74), and resting membrane potential ERev = − 22.4 ± 9.2 mV (mean ± S.D., n = 63).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings

claim: For non-rosette cells, input resistance Rm = 1.2 ± 1.2 GΩ (mean ± S.D., n = 74)
source: For non-rosette cells, we observed membrane capacitance Cm = 9.5 ± 6.2 pF (mean ± S.D., n = 74), input resistance Rm = 1.2 ± 1.2 GΩ (mean ± S.D., n = 74), and resting membrane potential ERev = − 22.4 ± 9.2 mV (mean ± S.D., n = 63).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings

claim: For non-rosette cells, resting membrane potential ERev = − 22.4 ± 9.2 mV (mean ± S.D., n = 63)
source: For non-rosette cells, we observed membrane capacitance Cm = 9.5 ± 6.2 pF (mean ± S.D., n = 74), input resistance Rm = 1.2 ± 1.2 GΩ (mean ± S.D., n = 74), and resting membrane potential ERev = − 22.4 ± 9.2 mV (mean ± S.D., n = 63).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings

claim: In approximately 21% of neural rosette cells (24 out of 111), applications of GABA induced inward currents
source: In approximately 21% of the cells (24 out of 111), applications of GABA induced inward currents.
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings

claim: GABA induced currents are sensitive to bicuculline
source: The GABA induced currents are sensitive to bicucculin (Bicu, 200 μM), but in some cases the application of 200 μM Bicu did not completely block the GABA induced currents (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by Figure 7B showing bicuculline blocking

claim: Selamectin induced inward currents in neural rosette cells
source: To determine whether selamectin regulates membrane electrophysiological properties in neural rosette cells, we analyzed responses of the whole-cell currents to the applications of selamectin. Selamectin indeed induced inward currents in neural rosette cells (Figure 7C), but the response was heterogeneous.
evidence: Supported by Figure 7C showing selamectin-induced currents

claim: Among 77 recorded neural rosette cells, 43 cells (64.2%) did not display induced currents by either GABA or selamectin
source: Among the 77 recorded cells, the largest group (43 cells, 64.2%) was those that did not display induced currents by either GABA or selamectin.
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings summarized in Figure 7D

claim: Among 77 recorded neural rosette cells, 14 cells (20.9%) displayed induced currents only by GABA
source: The second largest group (14 cells, 20.9%) is those that displayed induced currents only by GABA.
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings summarized in Figure 7D

claim: Among 77 recorded neural rosette cells, 10 cells (14.9%) displayed both GABA and selamectin induced currents
source: The third group (10 cells, 14.9%) was those that displayed both GABA and selamectin induced currents.
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings summarized in Figure 7D

claim: No neural rosette cells displayed only selamectin-induced currents
source: No cells displayed only selamectin-induced currents.
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings summarized in Figure 7D

claim: 27 out of 73 non-rosette cells (37%) displayed GABA induced currents
source: Slightly higher percentage (27 out of 73 cells, 37%) of non-rosette cells (Figure 7E) displayed GABA induced currents, which could be blocked by Bicu (Figure 7F).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings

claim: Out of 44 non-rosette cells tested for both GABA and selamectin, 20 cells (45.5%) displayed only GABA-induced currents
source: Out of 44 non-rosette cells that we tested both GABA and selamectin induced currents, the largest group (20 cells, 45.5%) was the one that displayed only GABA-induced currents.
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings summarized in Figure 7H

claim: Out of 44 non-rosette cells tested for both GABA and selamectin, 17 cells (38.6%) displayed neither GABA nor selamectin induced currents
source: The second group (17 cells, 38.6%) was the one that displayed neither GABA nor selamectin induced currents.
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings summarized in Figure 7H

claim: Out of 44 non-rosette cells tested for both GABA and selamectin, 7 cells (15.9%) displayed both GABA- and selamectin-induced currents
source: The third group (7 cells, 15.9%) displayed both GABA- and selamectin-induced currents.
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings summarized in Figure 7H

claim: No non-rosette cells displayed only selamectin-induced currents
source: Similar to neural rosette cells, no non-rosette cells displayed only selamectin-induced currents.
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings summarized in Figure 7H

claim: A subset of GABA-responsive neural rosette cells in mESC cultures respond to selamectin
source: Taken together, our results uncover considerable heterogeneity in the response of neural rosettes and young neurons to GABA or selamectin and indicate that a subset of GABA-responsive neural rosette cells in mESC cultures respond to selamectin.
evidence: Inferred from electrophysiological recordings showing heterogeneous responses

claim: GABA could promote neuronal differentiation in adult hippocampal progenitor cells
source: While one study shows that GABA could promote neuronal differentiation in adult hippocampal progenitor cells (Tozuka et al., 2005), another found an inhibitory role on neuronal production in the postnatal sub-ventricular zone (Liu et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tozuka et al., 2005

claim: GABA has an inhibitory role on neuronal production in the postnatal sub-ventricular zone
source: While one study shows that GABA could promote neuronal differentiation in adult hippocampal progenitor cells (Tozuka et al., 2005), another found an inhibitory role on neuronal production in the postnatal sub-ventricular zone (Liu et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2005

claim: Significantly fewer BrdU+ cells were detected in selamectin-treated groups, suggesting decreased proliferation
source: To further probe the mechanisms by which selamectin promotes neuronal differentiation, we performed BrdU incorporation experiment in mESC cultures on Day 11 after the treatment with selamectin for 4 days. Significantly fewer BrdU+ cells were detected in selamectin-treated groups, suggesting decreased proliferation (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: Supported by Figure 8A-B showing BrdU incorporation data

claim: Selamectin increases the expression of proneural genes ascl1 and neurod
source: We detected an increased expression of the proneural genes ascl1 and neurod, as well as the DA lineage- associated genes lmx1a, lmx1b, and nurr1 in Day 11 culture compared to Day 8 culture, and such increase was further enhanced by selamectin (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by Figure 8C showing qRT-PCR results

claim: Selamectin increases the expression of DA lineage-associated genes lmx1a, lmx1b, and nurr1
source: We detected an increased expression of the proneural genes ascl1 and neurod, as well as the DA lineage- associated genes lmx1a, lmx1b, and nurr1 in Day 11 culture compared to Day 8 culture, and such increase was further enhanced by selamectin (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by Figure 8C showing qRT-PCR results

claim: There was no significant difference in cell death between control and selamectin-treated cultures
source: On Day 14, TUNEL labeling was carried out. The result showed no significant difference in cell death between control and selamectin-treated cultures (Figure 8D–E), suggesting that alteration in cell death contributes little to selamectin's pro-neurogenic activity.
evidence: Supported by Figure 8D-E showing TUNEL staining results

claim: Alteration in cell death contributes little to selamectin's pro-neurogenic activity
source: On Day 14, TUNEL labeling was carried out. The result showed no significant difference in cell death between control and selamectin-treated cultures (Figure 8D–E), suggesting that alteration in cell death contributes little to selamectin's pro-neurogenic activity.
evidence: Inferred from lack of difference in TUNEL staining

claim: The cell cycle length exhibited no significant difference between DMSO- (25.61 ± 6.99 hr, n = 31) and selamectin-treated cells (24 ± 6.53 hr, n = 28)
source: We found that the cell cycle length exhibited no significant difference between DMSO- (25.61 ± 6.99 hr, n = 31) and selamectin-treated cells (24 ± 6.53 hr, n = 28) (Figure 9B, left panel, Videos 1, 2).
evidence: Supported by Figure 9B and time-lapse imaging data

claim: There was no difference in the number of cells within single clones between DMSO- (13.46 ± 4.14 cells per clone, n = 56 clones) and selamectin- (15.15 ± 4.67 per clone, n = 59 clones) treated groups
source: We also quantified the number of cells within single clones and detected no difference between DMSO- (13.46 ± 4.14 cells per clone, n = 56 clones) and selamectin- (15.15 ± 4.67 per clone, n = 59 clones) treated groups (Figure 9B, right panel).
evidence: Supported by Figure 9B showing clonal analysis data

claim: Selamectin does not change the cell cycle length or the proliferation rate of mESC-derived neural progenitors
source: The results suggest that selamectin does not change the cell cycle length or the proliferation rate of mESC-derived neural progenitors.
evidence: Inferred from clonal analysis showing no change in cell cycle length or clone size

claim: Clonal quantification showed a significant increase of NeuN+ neurons within single clones treated with selamectin
source: Clonal quantification of cell fates showed a significant increase of NeuN+ (or TH+) neurons and a concurrent decrease of Ki67+ progenitor cells within single clones treated with selamectin (Figure 9F).
evidence: Supported by Figure 9F showing clonal fate analysis

claim: Clonal quantification showed a significant increase of TH+ neurons within single clones treated with selamectin
source: Clonal quantification of cell fates showed a significant increase of NeuN+ (or TH+) neurons and a concurrent decrease of Ki67+ progenitor cells within single clones treated with selamectin (Figure 9F).
evidence: Supported by Figure 9F showing clonal fate analysis

claim: Clonal quantification showed a concurrent decrease of Ki67+ progenitor cells within single clones treated with selamectin
source: Clonal quantification of cell fates showed a significant increase of NeuN+ (or TH+) neurons and a concurrent decrease of Ki67+ progenitor cells within single clones treated with selamectin (Figure 9F).
evidence: Supported by Figure 9F showing clonal fate analysis

claim: Selamectin acts to promote progenitor cell cycle exit toward terminal differentiation
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that selamectin acts to promote progenitor cell cycle exit toward terminal differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from clonal analysis showing increased neurons and decreased Ki67+ cells without change in proliferation rate

claim: Treatment with selamectin (0.25 μM, 0.5 μM, 0.75 μM) significantly increased the percentage of total neurons in H9 hESCs compared to the DMSO-treated control
source: In agreement with the results from mESCs, treatment with selamectin (0.25 μM, 0.5 μM, 0.75 μM) significantly increased the percentage of total neurons, TH and 5-HT neurons compared to the DMSO-treated control in both H9 hESCs (Figure 10B–C) and hiPSCs (Figure 10D–E).
evidence: Supported by Figure 10B-C showing H9 hESC results

claim: Treatment with selamectin significantly increased the percentage of TH neurons in H9 hESCs compared to the DMSO-treated control

claim: There was an obvious increase of the overall HuC-GFP+ neurons in the selamectin-treated zebrafish embryos as compared to the DMSO control
source: We noted an obvious increase of the overall HuC-GFP+ neurons in the selamectin-treated embryos as compared to the DMSO control (Figure 11B).
evidence: Supported by Figure 11B showing zebrafish imaging

claim: Quantification of the midbrain cluster showed a highly significant difference between the selamectin-treated and the control zebrafish embryos (n =20, t-test, p<0.001)
source: Quantification of the midbrain cluster (boxed) showed a highly significant difference between the selamectin-treated and the control (Figure 11C, n =20, t-test, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by Figure 11C showing quantification

claim: The number of ventral forebrain DA neurons was significantly increased in selamectin-treated zebrafish embryos as compared to the DMSO control
source: We also examined the effect of selamectin on DA neurons, by treating embryos with selamectin from 8 hpf to 48 hpf followed by immunostaining with the anti-TH antibody (Figure 11A). The number of ventral forebrain DA neurons was significantly increased in selamectin-treated embryos as compared to the DMSO control (Figure 11D–E).
evidence: Supported by Figure 11D-E showing TH immunostaining in zebrafish

claim: Selamectin has pro-neurogenic activity in vivo
source: These results suggest that selamectin has pro-neurogenic activity in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from zebrafish experiments showing increased neurons

claim: Mild electrical stimulation influences mESCs to assume a neuronal fate
source: It has been previously reported that mild electrical stimulation influences mESCs to assume a neuronal fate (Yamada et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yamada et al., 2007

claim: GABA released by local interneurons promotes the exit of adult neural stem cells from quiescence
source: Recently, in the context of adult neurogenesis, GABA released by local interneurons has been shown to promote the exit of adult neural stem cells from quiescence (thereby promote their proliferation) (Song et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Song et al., 2012

claim: Single neural rosette cell recordings reveal heterogeneous responses among progenitors to GABA and selamectin
source: Our single neural rosette cell recordings, which reveal the heterogeneous responses among progenitors, provide an explanation as to why the influence of GABA signaling on neurogenesis appears cell type- and context-dependent.
evidence: Inferred from electrophysiological recordings showing heterogeneity

claim: The influence of GABA signaling on neurogenesis appears cell type- and context-dependent
source: Our single neural rosette cell recordings, which reveal the heterogeneous responses among progenitors, provide an explanation as to why the influence of GABA signaling on neurogenesis appears cell type- and context-dependent.
evidence: Inferred from heterogeneous responses and literature showing contradictory effects

claim: Selamectin-potentiated activation of the γ2-containing GABAA receptor in mESC-derived neural progenitor cells causes Cl− outflow
source: These molecular and cellular findings, together with the pharmacogenetic and electrophysiological studies, lead us to propose that selamectin-potentiated activation of the γ2-containing GABAA receptor in mESC-derived neural progenitor cells causes Cl− outflow (due to the high internal chloride levels in these progenitor cells), thereby leading to the depolarization of neural progenitors and calcium influx.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on integration of multiple experimental findings

claim: Selamectin-induced Cl− outflow leads to the depolarization of neural progenitors and calcium influx
source: These molecular and cellular findings, together with the pharmacogenetic and electrophysiological studies, lead us to propose that selamectin-potentiated activation of the γ2-containing GABAA receptor in mESC-derived neural progenitor cells causes Cl− outflow (due to the high internal chloride levels in these progenitor cells), thereby leading to the depolarization of neural progenitors and calcium influx.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on integration of multiple experimental findings

claim: Depolarization and calcium influx activates proneural and lineage-specific transcription factors
source: This further activates proneural and lineage-specific transcription factors, which have established roles in promoting cell cycle exit toward terminal neuronal differentiation (Bertrand et al., 2002) (Figure 8F).
evidence: Proposed mechanism supported by citation to Bertrand et al., 2002 and illustrated in Figure 8F

claim: Proneural and lineage-specific transcription factors have established roles in promoting cell cycle exit toward terminal neuronal differentiation

claim: Neural activity-dependent regulation of transcription factor expression is an evolutionarily conserved phenomenon

source: It is worth pointing out that our screen of 2000 compounds was not successful in identifying chemicals that specifically increase DA neuronal production, suggesting that these compounds may be rare, and large compound libraries need to be screened in order to find them.
evidence: Based on screening results
